notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Acts 18, drawn from the sources accessible through the approved sites.

---

## ACTS 18 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### v. 1 — Paul left Athens and went to Corinth

**Traditional reading:** After his mixed reception before the Athenian philosophers, Paul walked roughly 50 miles west to Corinth, a major commercial hub famous for its wealth and immorality. In classical Greek, "to act like a Corinthian" meant to practice fornication, and a "Corinthian companion" meant a prostitute. The immoral reputation stemmed from the worship of Aphrodite, whose temple employed over a thousand ritual prostitutes. Yet Paul chose Corinth precisely because its crossroads location meant a strong church there could reach the whole Empire. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-18-commentary)

Gill notes that Corinth lay between two seas (the Aegean and Ionian), had been destroyed by Rome in 146 B.C. and rebuilt by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony. Paul arrived weak and fearful, as he later described in 1 Corinthians 2:1–3. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/18.htm)

**Baptist:** The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary observes that Paul was likely discouraged after Athens, noting that "the cold, mocking tone of Athenian philosophers was as discouraging to Paul as the scourgings, stonings and imprisonments of the Jewish mobs." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/acts-18.html)

---

### v. 2 — Aquila and Priscilla, expelled from Rome under Claudius

**Traditional reading:** Paul found a Jewish couple, Aquila (a native of Pontus) and Priscilla, recently arrived from Italy because Emperor Claudius had expelled all Jews from Rome. The Roman historian Suetonius records that Claudius banished Jews because they "indulged in constant riots at the instigation of Chrestus" — likely a garbled reference to Christ, suggesting the expulsion (c. A.D. 49) arose from Jewish-Christian disputes in Rome's synagogues. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

Gill notes that Aquila is a Latin name meaning "eagle"; his Hebrew name may have been "Nesher." Priscilla is a diminutive of Prisca, a name belonging to a great Roman family. In half of the New Testament mentions of this couple, Priscilla's name is listed first — unusual for the era and perhaps indicating her high social standing or prominence in ministry. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/18.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/)

---

### v. 3 — Paul stayed and worked with them as tentmakers

**Traditional reading:** Paul shared their trade of tentmaking (leather-working). In Judaism, rabbis were not permitted to receive payment for teaching, so they practiced a trade. Paul voluntarily supported himself, though he affirmed his apostolic right to financial support (1 Cor. 9:7–14), so that no one could accuse him of preaching for profit. Modern missions calls this "tentmaking ministry." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

Gill explains the Greek word for "tentmakers" could refer to makers of soldier's tents from leather or sackcloth, or to makers of linen canopies used as sun-shades, or even tapestry for theatres and palaces. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/18.htm)

---

### v. 4 — Paul reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath

**Traditional reading:** Paul "reasoned" (discussed, debated from the Scriptures) every Sabbath, seeking to persuade both Jews and the "Greeks" — Gentile God-fearers who attended synagogue. This was his consistent pattern: to the Jew first, then to the Greek. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-18-commentary)

Gill notes that Paul was diligent and indefatigable: on weekdays he laboured with his hands, and every Sabbath he preached Christ. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/18.htm)

---

### v. 5 — Silas and Timothy arrive; Paul devoted himself fully to the word

**Traditional reading:** When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, they brought good news about the Thessalonians' steadfast faith (1 Thess. 3:6–10), which greatly encouraged Paul. Timothy may also have brought financial support from the Philippian church (2 Cor. 11:8–9), allowing Paul to set aside tentmaking and devote himself fully to preaching that "Jesus is the Christ." The BSB footnote reading "Paul devoted himself fully to the word" reflects the sense of the Greek, where Paul was "compelled" or "pressed in spirit" to testify. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/)

Gill observes that some manuscripts read "in speech" rather than "in spirit," meaning Paul was "instant in preaching" — he preached more frequently and fervently with his co-workers' arrival. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/18.htm)

---

### v. 6 — Opposition, blasphemy, and Paul's dramatic turning to the Gentiles

**Traditional reading:** When the Corinthian Jews "opposed and insulted him" (literally "blasphemed"), Paul shook out his garments — a dramatic gesture so that not even synagogue dust would remain on his clothes — and declared, "Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent." This echoes Ezekiel 33:4, where the watchman is free of bloodguilt if he has sounded the warning. Paul then announced his turn to the Gentiles, fulfilling the spirit of Jesus' words in Matthew 7:6 about not casting pearls before swine. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

Gill says the blasphemy was directed against both Christ and the apostle; the Jews "contradicted themselves" and their own Scriptures. The phrase "I am clean" means Paul had discharged his duty as a preacher and delivered his own soul. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/18.htm)

---

### vv. 7–8 — Paul moves next door; Crispus and many Corinthians believe

**Traditional reading:** Paul left the synagogue and moved his ministry base to the house of Titus Justus, a God-fearing Gentile whose house was "next door" to the synagogue — a provocative location. The synagogue ruler Crispus and his entire household believed and were baptized. Paul personally baptized Crispus (1 Cor. 1:14). Many Corinthians hearing the message also believed and were baptized, laying the foundation of the Corinthian church. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

Gill notes the significance of believers' baptism: "first they heard…then they believed…and upon their believing, they are baptized." He traces the history of the Corinthian church through the centuries, noting its bishops into the seventh century. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/18.htm)

---

### vv. 9–10 — The Lord's vision: "Do not be afraid… I have many people in this city"

**Traditional reading:** The Lord Jesus appeared to Paul in a night vision. The command "Do not be afraid" implies Paul was genuinely fearful — possibly fearing a repeat of the violence he suffered in Thessalonica and Berea, or moral discouragement from Corinth's darkness. The solution to fear was obedience: "keep on speaking; do not be silent." Jesus gave three assurances: His presence ("I am with you"), His protection ("no one will lay a hand on you"), and His sovereign election ("I have many people in this city"). The last phrase refers to those not yet converted — God's elect in Corinth who would yet believe. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

**Reformed:** The phrase "I have many people in this city" is understood in Reformed theology as a reference to God's elect — those chosen before the foundation of the world who will certainly come to faith. Gill writes: "Christ has a people who are related to him, and he has an interest in, before they are effectually called by grace." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/18.htm)

**Baptist:** Spurgeon, cited by Guzik, emphasized three things in the promise "I am with you": the presence of Jesus, the sympathy of Jesus, and the cooperation of Jesus. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

---

### v. 11 — Paul stayed a year and a half, teaching the word of God

**Traditional reading:** This was Paul's longest stay in any city where he founded a church up to that point. His ministry is described simply as "teaching the word of God." Paul was not merely an evangelist making quick converts; he was committed to making mature disciples. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes that Paul established what might be called "Bible Schools" in four locations: Antioch (one year), Corinth (a year and a half), Ephesus (two years), and Rome (two years). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/acts-18.html)

---

### vv. 12–13 — The Jews bring Paul before Gallio

**Traditional reading:** When Gallio was proconsul of Achaia (c. A.D. 51–52, a detail that helps date Paul's ministry), the Jews "coordinated an attack" (literally "rose up with one accord") and brought Paul before the judgment seat (bēma). Their charge was that Paul was "persuading people to worship God in ways contrary to the law." By "the law" they likely meant Roman law, hoping Gallio would see Christianity as an illegal religion. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/)

**Historical note:** Gallio was the brother of Seneca the philosopher. His contemporaries called him "the agreeable Gallio." Both he and Seneca were later put to death by Nero. The bēma was a large elevated speaker's platform in the Corinthian agora. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/acts-18.html; https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-18-commentary)

---

### vv. 14–16 — Gallio's dismissal: "settle it yourselves"

**Traditional reading:** Before Paul could even defend himself, Gallio dismissed the case. He recognized that the dispute was not about criminal wrongdoing but about "words and names and your own law" — a purely internal Jewish religious dispute. His refusal to judge made a crucial legal precedent: Christianity was, in effect, treated as a lawful religion (religio licita) under Roman rule, protecting Paul's ministry throughout the provinces. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary says Gallio "respected the premise of separation of duties and obligations of persons, to God and to Caesar" (Matt. 22:21). He "simply, dutifully, with integrity, laid down the proper limits of his office." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/acts-18.html)

---

### v. 17 — The crowd beats Sosthenes; Gallio is unconcerned

**Traditional reading:** The "crowd" (likely Greeks, as some manuscripts specify) seized Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler who had replaced Crispus, and beat him in front of the bēma. Gallio "was of no concern" — he looked the other way. Spurgeon remarked, "It was his duty to let this good man alone, but it was not his duty to allow the Gentiles, on the other hand, to begin beating the Jews." Sosthenes may later have become a Christian, since a "Sosthenes" appears as co-author of 1 Corinthians (1 Cor. 1:1). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

---

### v. 18 — Paul's vow at Cenchrea; departure for Syria

**Traditional reading:** Paul remained "quite some time" after the Gallio incident — he was not forced out of Corinth. Before sailing for Syria, he had his head shaved at Cenchrea (Corinth's eastern port) "to keep a vow he had made." This is almost certainly a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), involving a period of consecration during which one abstains from wine, avoids corpses, and lets hair grow uncut. The shaving marked the vow's completion; the hair would be offered at the temple in Jerusalem. Paul's urgency to reach Jerusalem (v. 21) was to present this offering at the feast. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

Ellicott clarifies that the Greek word here for "shorn" differs from "shaving" in 1 Cor. 11:6; it was lawful for a Nazirite to crop his hair during the vow, and the shorn hair was to be taken to the temple and burned. This explains Paul's eagerness to keep the feast at Jerusalem. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/18.htm)

**Traditional reading on Paul's Jewish practice:** Paul's observance of a Nazirite vow demonstrates he was not anti-Jewish. Though he adamantly opposed requiring Gentile converts to observe Jewish ceremonies, he saw nothing wrong with Jewish believers voluntarily observing such forms, provided they recognized their fulfilment in Christ. The intense worldliness of Corinth may have stirred Paul to express special consecration to God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/)

---

### vv. 19–21 — Brief stop in Ephesus; "I will return if God is willing"

**Traditional reading:** Paul, Priscilla, and Aquila reached Ephesus. Paul left the couple there (likely at his request, to continue the work) and entered the synagogue to reason with the Jews. The Ephesians asked him to stay longer, but he declined, needing to reach Jerusalem for the feast to complete his vow. Paul had wanted to evangelize Ephesus two years earlier but was prevented by the Holy Spirit (Acts 16:6); now the Spirit gave him liberty. His parting words — "I will come back to you if God is willing" — model the proper submission of all plans to God's will (cf. James 4:15). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

---

### v. 22 — Paul lands at Caesarea, goes up to Jerusalem, returns to Antioch

**Traditional reading:** "Gone up and greeted the church" means Paul went up to Jerusalem (elevated geographically and spiritually) and likely completed his Nazirite vow at the temple. Then he "went down" to Antioch in Syria, his sending church, concluding his second missionary journey. This journey had lasted roughly three years. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

---

### v. 23 — Paul strengthens disciples in Galatia and Phrygia (third journey begins)

**Traditional reading:** After an unspecified time in Antioch, Paul began his third missionary journey by revisiting churches founded earlier — congregations in Tarsus, Derbe, Lystra, Iconium, and Pisidian Antioch. His priority was "strengthening all the disciples," demonstrating his commitment to disciple-making, not merely conversion. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

---

### v. 24 — Apollos arrives in Ephesus

**Traditional reading:** While Paul travelled through Galatia and Phrygia, a Jew named Apollos arrived in Ephesus. He was from Alexandria — a major centre of Jewish learning and home to Philo. Luke describes him as "eloquent" (Greek logios, which can mean either "learned" or "eloquent"; the Pulpit Commentary notes both meanings are possible) and "mighty in the Scriptures" — thoroughly knowledgeable in the Old Testament, especially messianic prophecies. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/18-24.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/)

Gill observes that Apollos is a Greek name though he was a Jew by birth; some identify him with Apelles (Rom. 16:10). "Mighty in the Scriptures" is a Jewish phrase also applied to Ahithophel ("mighty in the law"). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/18.htm; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/18-24.htm)

---

### v. 25 — Apollos: instructed, fervent, accurate — but knowing only John's baptism

**Traditional reading:** Apollos had been "instructed in the way of the Lord" and was "fervent in spirit" (literally "boiling in spirit" — bubbling over with enthusiasm). He "spoke and taught accurately about Jesus," yet he "knew only the baptism of John." This means he likely preached that the Messiah had come and called for repentance, but his knowledge of Jesus' full person, death, resurrection, and the coming of the Holy Spirit was incomplete. The widespread knowledge of John the Baptist's ministry is evident from reaching as far as Alexandria. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic:** The phrase "fervent in spirit" receives emphasis. David Guzik (Enduring Word, a charismatic-leaning source) highlights that Apollos taught what he knew with bold passion — "he didn't know much about Jesus, but what he did know genuinely excited him." The emphasis is on Spirit-empowered fervour, not mere intellectual skill. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/)

---

### v. 26 — Priscilla and Aquila explain "the way of God more accurately"

**Traditional reading:** When Priscilla and Aquila heard Apollos speaking boldly in the synagogue, they "took him in" (privately, not publicly shaming him) and "explained the way of God more accurately." This is a model of gracious mentoring: a gifted, eloquent, fervent preacher lacked full knowledge, and an ordinary tentmaking couple filled the gap. Significantly, Priscilla is named first again, suggesting she played a leading role in the instruction. Ellicott comments that Priscilla's prominence "implies that she was a woman of more than ordinary culture, a student of the older Scriptures, able, with a prophetic insight, to help even the disciple of Philo to understand them better." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/18.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/)

---

### vv. 27–28 — Apollos crosses to Achaia and powerfully refutes the Jews

**Traditional reading:** When Apollos desired to go to Achaia (Corinth), the Ephesian brothers encouraged him and wrote a letter of commendation. In Achaia, he "greatly helped those who by grace had believed" and "powerfully refuted the Jews in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ." Gill says Apollos's reasoning was "so strong and nervous, his arguments so weighty and powerful" that the Jews could not stand against him. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/18.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/)

**Note on the Corinthians' factionalism:** Apollos later became the figurehead of a faction in Corinth (1 Cor. 1:12; 3:4–6), though this was not his doing. Paul held him in high esteem and urged him to revisit Corinth (1 Cor. 16:12; Titus 3:13). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/18-24.htm)

---

## WHERE PROTESTANT TRADITIONS DIFFER

### The vow of v. 18 (Nazirite vow)

**Reformed / Evangelical:** See the vow as a legitimate expression of Jewish piety that Paul, as a Jewish believer, voluntarily undertook. It demonstrates continuity with Old Testament forms without imposing them on Gentiles. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/)

**Some Holiness/Wesleyan traditions:** Emphasise the Nazirite vow as a model of personal consecration and separation from the world — a "special dedication" to God, relevant as a pattern for believers seeking deeper holiness. This is an application rather than a denominational dispute.

---

### "I have many people in this city" (v. 10)

**Reformed (Gill, Spurgeon):** "Many people" refers to God's elect — those chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world, not yet converted but certain to be called. God's foreknowledge and predestination guarantee the success of evangelism. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/18.htm; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/acts/acts-18.cfm)

**Wesleyan/Arminian:** Would stress that God's "people" are those He foreknows will respond to the gospel in faith. The promise assures Paul that many in Corinth are open to the message, not that individuals are predestined irrespective of their free response.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** David Guzik does not heavily press the predestination angle, focusing instead on the practical encouragement: God's sovereign knowledge of the outcome should embolden fearful preachers. The emphasis falls on divine assurance and persevering in mission. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/)

---

### Apollos and the baptism of John (vv. 25–26)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic:** Some in these traditions see Acts 18:25–19:7 as evidence that Apollos (and the "disciples" in Acts 19) had an incomplete experience — knowing John's baptism of repentance but not Christian baptism in the Spirit. This underscores the importance of subsequent Spirit-baptism beyond initial belief. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-18/)

**Reformed/Baptist:** Generally see Apollos as a genuine believer with incomplete doctrinal knowledge, not as someone lacking the Holy Spirit. His deficiency was in understanding, not in spiritual experience. Priscilla and Aquila's gentle correction was doctrinal, not an impartation of the Spirit.
